title: Menstrualome aids difficult endometriosis diagnosis - Nature Biotechnology
gist: Only the opening line of this feature is outside the paywall: biotech companies are pursuing radically divergent biomarker classes — from circulating microRNAs to menstrual-fluid transcriptomics — to build a diagnostic for a disease that still has no clear molecular definition. The extractable signal is the structure of the bet, not the data: multiple incompatible technical approaches competing to define the standard for endometriosis diagnosis.

insights.claim: Biotech companies chasing endometriosis diagnostics have converged on no common analyte, spanning circulating microRNAs at one extreme and menstrual-fluid transcriptomics at the other.
insights.speaker: Carrie Arnold
insights.so_what: Radical technical divergence means the category has no incumbent standard yet — high option value on whichever assay class validates first, and high write-off risk for the rest.
insights.quote: From circulating microRNAs to menstrual-fluid transcriptomics, biotech companies are betting on radically different biomarkers

insights.claim: The disease being targeted still lacks a clear molecular definition, so diagnostic developers are effectively being asked to define the disease and detect it at the same time.
insights.speaker: Carrie Arnold
insights.so_what: Without a molecular gold standard there is no clean regulatory endpoint to validate against — the core reason these programs carry unusually long timelines.
insights.quote: a disease that still lacks a clear molecular definition

insights.claim: Menstrual fluid is being treated as a sampling compartment in its own right rather than waste, opening a non-invasive specimen type for conditions currently diagnosed only by surgery.
insights.speaker: Carrie Arnold
insights.so_what: A new accessible specimen class can create a diagnostics market where sampling cost previously blocked one — watch for adjacent indications using the same fluid.
